args.text: [lane-wren] Three risks of keeping DNS (Domain Name System) answers cached for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing failures. (2) Slow recovery: when a service fails over to a backup address, cached old answers delay the switch. (3) Security exposure: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache longer, so harm lasts longer before it expires.

args.text: [lane-wren] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so the sender must be able to try again safely. If repeating a request gives the same result as sending it once, a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate orders or other repeated side effects.

args.text: [lane-wren] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, double a common 8-byte integer key, so indexes and tables grow larger. (2) Information leak: it embeds the creation time, so anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the record was made. The upside is that it sorts by time, which keeps database inserts efficient.

args.text: [lane-wren] A write-ahead log is a record of intended changes that a database saves to durable storage before it changes the main data files. If the system crashes, it replays this log on restart, so completed work is kept and half-finished work can be undone.

args.text: [lane-wren] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: if the client changes between runs, a difference in results may come from the client rather than the system being tested. (2) Repeatability: others, or you at a later date, can rerun the test with the same software and expect comparable results.

args.text: [lane-wren] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal producers to slow down or stop when consumers cannot keep up. It stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make delays worse, by making senders wait, drop work or be refused.

args.text: [lane-wren] Two ways a cron (timed job scheduler) job can run twice: (1) Overlap: a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts. (2) Duplicate hosts: the same schedule is installed on more than one server, so each runs it. One guard: take a lock, for example a database or file lock, at the start, and exit if another run already holds it.

args.text: [lane-wren] A tombstone is a marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. It tells every copy that the item was removed, so a replica that missed the delete does not bring the old value back. Tombstones are cleaned up only after a set time, once all copies should have seen them.

args.text: [lane-wren] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) Mixed results on the same code: it passes on some runs and fails on others with no change to the code or the test. (2) Timing or order dependence: it fails only under load, on certain machines, or when tests run in a different order, and often passes when simply rerun.

args.text: [lane-wren] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock only until a set time. Clock skew means machines disagree about the time, so a holder whose clock runs slow may think it still has the lock after the lock service has given it to someone else. Then two holders act at once, which breaks the lock's purpose. Fencing tokens, which are rising numbers checked by the protected resource, reduce this risk.

args.text: [lane-wren] Two costs of very long feature branches: (1) Painful merges: the longer the branch lives, the more the main code changes underneath it, so conflicts pile up and take time to resolve. (2) Late feedback: large changes get reviewed and tested together only at the end, so problems are found late, are harder to trace, and cost more to fix.

args.text: [lane-wren] A canary release sends a new version to a small share of real traffic first, and checks whether it behaves well compared with the current version. It watches signs such as error rates, response times and resource use, so a bad release can be stopped or rolled back before most users are affected.

[lane-wren] Two risks of storing secrets in environment variables: (1) They leak easily, because they can appear in crash reports, debug logs, process listings and child processes that inherit them. (2) They are hard to control and rotate, since anyone or anything that can read the process environment can see them, and changing a value usually needs a restart.

args.text: [lane-wren] Latency is the time a request takes to get a response. The p50 (50th percentile, or median) is the time that half of requests beat, so it shows the typical experience. The p99 (99th percentile) is the time that 99 in every 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that a small share of users still meet. A service can have a good p50 and a poor p99.

args.text: [lane-wren] A cache hit rate is the share of requests answered from the cache instead of the slower source. Two reasons it can drop after a deploy: (1) The cache starts empty or cold, for example because servers restart with in-memory caches, so early requests all miss until it refills. (2) The key format or data shape changes, so new requests look for keys that old entries do not match, and the old entries are never used.

args.text: [lane-wren] Head-of-line blocking is when the item at the front of a queue is stuck or slow, so everything behind it must wait, even if those items are ready to go. Picture one slow customer at a till holding up the whole line. In networks, one lost packet can hold back later packets on the same connection until it is resent.
